Demand for cooling is overtaking demand for heating for the first time in energy history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its World Energy Outlook 2026 on Thursday.

The agency’s first annual outlook since the Iran war upended energy markets and forecasts found that higher temperatures, extreme heat waves in previously cooler regions, and higher incomes are driving a surge in air-conditioning use.

“Already today, for the first time in energy history, demand for cooling in buildings is overtaking that for heating,” the IEA said.

Cooling demand is set to jump by 1,700 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2035 in the agency’s baseline Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS). But in the heatwave case, the increase is 40% higher, or an extra 700 TWh in additional demand, with particularly strong implications for peak demand.

While the global energy system has so far shown remarkable resilience in the face of the Hormuz crisis, the worst supply disruption in the history of oil markets, the longer the current crisis lasts, the deeper the scars and consequences will be, the IEA said.

It’s too soon for grand conclusions on how energy policies will change, but “some general conclusions are clear, chief among them being a reinforced focus on energy security and affordability as guiding principles for energy decision-making,” the agency said.

“In many cases, especially among fuel importers, these concerns are closely aligned with the push for clean energy transitions.”

The central question in the World Energy Outlook 2026 is how the Hormuz crisis might alter policy preferences, risk perceptions, and the mix of fuels and technologies to meet energy needs.

Whatever path the world takes, higher incomes and a growing population are expected to boost demand for the services that energy provides, including mobility, heating, cooling, and computing power, the agency said.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol.
